html:
SMTO-UI-0044 — Command rules can't include specific options or file names

GUID: 92d98626-dd9f-44c5-b547-f82a7ef4536e
Slug: ui-permission-argument-unsupported
Domain: UI · Subsystem: ui

What happened

  • A saved command rule can only name a program and one of its known actions, such as "git commit". It can't include extra options, file names or other details, so this rule wasn't added.

How to fix — simple steps

  1. In Shell command permissions, type only the program name (for example docker) or the program plus a known action (for example git commit), with no options or file names, then select Add rule. Rules match whole kinds of commands, and options like -m or file names aren't allowed in them.
  2. If the program's action isn't accepted, type just the program name on its own, without a folder path. Only common actions of programs like git, docker and npm are recognized, but a plain program name on its own is allowed.
  3. For one exact command, wait for SMTO to ask about it during a task and select Approve once. Approve once covers that exact command without creating a rule that would allow it every time.

What success looks like

  • The rule appears in the Shell command permissions list and Apply saves without an error.

If it still fails

  • Select Copy error details and send them to the person who manages SMTO, with the text you typed for the rule.

Technical details

Observed condition

  • A shell permission rule was rejected because its executable or argv_prefix is malformed, has more than 4 prefix tokens, has unknown fields, or uses a token outside the supported executable/subcommand family list.

What this means

  • A shell rule uses invalid executable structure, unsupported argv-prefix tokens/length, unknown fields or a token outside the supported command family. The shown control rejects this local action before its dependent submission. Earlier requests and saved state are unaffected by this validation result; server-side authority remains authoritative.

Why this can happen

  • A shell rule uses invalid executable structure, unsupported argv-prefix tokens/length, unknown fields or a token outside the supported command family.

How to diagnose it

  • Compare executable and subcommand prefix with supported structural families.

How to fix it

  • permission_policy.js canonical() throws ui_permission_argument_unsupported (ShellPermissionRule.structural_family raises server-side) when a shell rule's executable fails ^[a-zA-Z0-9_][a-zA-Z0-9_.+-]{0,63}$, argv_prefix exceeds 4 tokens, or a token is not in SHELL_FAMILIES/SHELL_SUBFAMILIES. Use an executable alone or a supported executable/subcommand family; approve argument-specific operations per action with Approve once.
  • Use a supported executable/subcommand family. Use the existing Approve once flow for argument-specific authorization.

Retry and execution caution

  • Correct the recorded cause, then inspect current state and existing receipts before requesting another attempt.

How to verify the fix

  • A supported family rule validates, with one-time approval used for argument-specific authority.

What not to do

  • Do not bypass the unsupported-feature check or reinterpret an unsupported response as success.

Technical notes

  • The shown control rejects this local action before its dependent submission. Earlier requests and saved state are unaffected by this validation result; server-side authority remains authoritative.
  • Preserve the occurrence ID and safe request/operation references. Receipts and occurrence facts establish what started or completed; the catalog does not authorize retries or establish execution outcome.
